name: Economic Profit
expression: π = TR − TC = TR − explicit costs − implicit costs
meaning: Measures value created after charging all resources their opportunity cost.
intuition: A positive result means the firm beats the next-best use of its resources.
workedExample: Revenue is €500,000, explicit cost is €390,000, and implicit cost is €80,000. Economic profit is €30,000.
commonMistake: Omitting owner-supplied capital or labor because it creates no recorded invoice.
relatedLearningOutcome: determine and interpret breakeven and shutdown points of production, as well as how economies and diseconomies of scale affect costs under perfect and imperfect competition

name: Total Revenue
meaning: The sales proceeds from selling Q units at price P per unit.
intuition: Revenue combines the price earned on each unit with the number of units sold.
workedExample: At €32 per unit and 4,500 units, total revenue is €144,000.
commonMistake: Treating price as marginal revenue under downward-sloping demand.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain supply and demand relationships under monopolistic competition, including the optimal price and output for firms as well as pricing strategy

name: Average Total and Variable Cost
expression: ATC = TC / Q; AVC = VC / Q
meaning: Cost per unit using total cost or variable cost, respectively.
intuition: ATC supports the breakeven test; AVC supports the short-run shutdown test.
workedExample: At Q=2,000, TC is €50,000 and VC is €34,000. ATC is €25 and AVC is €17.
commonMistake: Using ATC instead of AVC to decide whether to shut down temporarily.
relatedLearningOutcome: determine and interpret breakeven and shutdown points of production, as well as how economies and diseconomies of scale affect costs under perfect and imperfect competition

name: Unit Breakeven Quantity
meaning: Units needed for total contribution to cover fixed cost when unit price and variable cost are constant.
intuition: Each unit contributes P−V toward the fixed-cost hurdle.
workedExample: FC €96,000, P €52, V €28 gives contribution €24 and breakeven of 4,000 units.
commonMistake: Applying the formula when P−V is zero or negative.
relatedLearningOutcome: determine and interpret breakeven and shutdown points of production, as well as how economies and diseconomies of scale affect costs under perfect and imperfect competition

name: Profit-Maximizing Output Condition
expression: MR = MC, with MC rising through MR
meaning: Identifies an interior output at which the last unit's incremental benefit equals incremental cost.
intuition: Expand while the next unit adds more revenue than cost, then stop when that advantage disappears.
workedExample: If MR=84−2Q and MC=24, equality gives Q=30; confirm MC does not cross MR from above.
commonMistake: Using equality without checking that it represents a maximum or reading price from MR.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain supply and demand relationships under monopolistic competition, including the optimal price and output for firms as well as pricing strategy

name: Marginal Revenue for Linear Demand
expression: If P = a − bQ, then MR = a − 2bQ
meaning: For a single-price seller with linear demand, marginal revenue shares the price intercept and has twice the slope magnitude.
intuition: Selling an extra unit requires a price reduction that affects earlier units, so MR falls faster than price.
workedExample: Demand P=90−0.5Q implies MR=90−Q. With MC=30, Q*=60 and P*=60.
commonMistake: Doubling the intercept instead of the slope coefficient.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain supply and demand relationships under monopolistic competition, including the optimal price and output for firms as well as pricing strategy

name: Contribution and Operating Profit
meaning: Separates unit contribution from the fixed-cost hurdle in a linear cost model.
intuition: Every unit first pays its own variable cost; the remainder covers fixed cost and then profit.
workedExample: P €40, V €22, Q 7,000, FC €100,000 yields contribution €126,000 and profit €26,000.
commonMistake: Calling contribution profit before subtracting fixed cost.
relatedLearningOutcome: determine and interpret breakeven and shutdown points of production, as well as how economies and diseconomies of scale affect costs under perfect and imperfect competition

name: N-Firm Concentration Ratio
meaning: Adds the market shares of the N largest firms.

variables.s_i: market share of ranked firm i

intuition: It shows how much of the defined market the leading group controls but ignores the distribution inside that group.
workedExample: Top shares of 28%, 21%, 17%, and 9% give CR4 of 75%.
commonMistake: Comparing ratios that use different N values or different market definitions.
relatedLearningOutcome: identify the type of market structure within which a firm operates and describe the use and limitations of concentration measures

name: Herfindahl–Hirschman Index
meaning: Sums squared market shares, giving larger firms greater influence on the concentration measure.
intuition: Squaring highlights heavyweight firms and uses the full share distribution when all firms are included.
workedExample: Shares 50%, 30%, and 20% produce HHI=2,500+900+400=3,800, or 0.38 with decimal shares.
relatedLearningOutcome: identify the type of market structure within which a firm operates and describe the use and limitations of concentration measures

name: Two-Firm Merger Change in HHI
meaning: Measures the HHI increase when firms with shares a and b combine, holding other shares constant.
intuition: The cross-product terms appear when the combined share is squared.
workedExample: Firms with 14% and 8% shares merge; ΔHHI=2×14×8=224 percentage-share points.
commonMistake: Using shares on different scales or applying the shortcut when market shares themselves change for other reasons.
relatedLearningOutcome: identify the type of market structure within which a firm operates and describe the use and limitations of concentration measures

name: Cournot Symmetric Duopoly Equilibrium
expression: For demand P = a − b(q1+q2) and constant MC = c: q1* = q2* = (a − c)/(3b); Q* = 2(a − c)/(3b); P* = (a + 2c)/3
meaning: Solves the simultaneous best-response (reaction) functions of two symmetric Cournot competitors for equilibrium output and price.
intuition: Each firm produces less as it expects the rival to produce more; solving both reaction functions together pins down a stable output between the monopoly and perfectly competitive levels.
workedExample: Demand P=450−Q with constant MC=30 (a=450, b=1, c=30): each firm produces (450−30)/3=140, aggregate output is 280, and price is 450−280=170.
commonMistake: Solving only one firm's reaction function while treating the rival's output as permanently fixed, instead of solving the two reaction functions simultaneously; or substituting aggregate Q instead of one firm's qi into the price equation.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain supply and demand relationships under oligopoly, including the optimal price and output for firms as well as pricing strategy

name: HHI Equal-Share Equivalent Firm Count
expression: If M firms hold equal shares, HHI = 1/M (decimal scale); equivalently M = 1/HHI
meaning: Benchmarks an observed HHI against the number of equal-sized competitors that would produce the same index value.

variables.M: number of equal-share firms implied by the index
variables.HHI: Herfindahl–Hirschman Index on a decimal share scale (shares sum to 1)

intuition: Equal shares minimize HHI for a given firm count, so 1/HHI is a useful, conservative read on the effective number of competitors implied by the index.
workedExample: An HHI of 0.20 on a decimal scale is analogous to a market shared equally by 1/0.20=5 firms.
commonMistake: Applying the benchmark to an unequal-share market as if it reported the true firm count rather than an equal-share equivalent, or mixing percentage-scale and decimal-scale HHI when solving for M.
relatedLearningOutcome: identify the type of market structure within which a firm operates and describe the use and limitations of concentration measures
